content.title: About
content.content: Canned beets are cooked beet roots packed in glass or metal jars with a small amount of water and salt, but with reduced sodium. The beets retain their bright red color, sweet‑earthy flavor, and most of their nutrients, ready to eat straight from the can.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beets contain betaine, which supports liver function and helps lower homocysteine levels.
The deep red hue comes from betanin, a powerful antioxidant.
Canning allows storage for 2‑3 years without major loss of B‑vitamins and minerals.
Reduced‑sodium versions are better suited for people monitoring blood pressure.
Beets are featured in many traditional dishes: Russian vinaigrette, American beet salad with walnuts, and Middle Eastern salads.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Betanin and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Nitrates in beets help dilate blood vessels and may lower blood pressure.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt makes the product safer for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Beet allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to beets.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Beets are naturally sweet; those monitoring blood glucose should account for the carbs.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some brands add preservatives; check the ingredient list if you have sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned beets can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, soups, snacks, or used as a side dish. They pair well with olive oil, balsamic vinegar, nuts, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the beets in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 5‑7 days. Discard if the can is bulging, the beets develop an off‑odor, or the color changes dramatically.

greens-ns-as-to-form-cooked.title: Greens, NS as to form, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Greens, NS as to form, cooked (4355) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from a blend of leafy greens that have been gently boiled. The process retains most nutrients, gives a soft texture and a neutral flavor, making it a versatile ingredient for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is produced from a mix of spinach, kale, and Swiss chard leaves.
Boiling is performed at 85–90 °C for 3–5 minutes, preserving bright colour and most vitamins.
Greens, NS as to form, cooked is often used in baby foods because of its mild texture and low acidity.
The product contains no added sugar, salt or preservatives.
Packaging is made from biodegradable material suitable for composting.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Leafy greens provide vitamins B6, B9 (folate) and B2, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Quercetin, lutein and carotenoids in the product help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The retained dietary fibre promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: One cup of the product contains about 30 kcal, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Potassium, magnesium and iron are present, supporting muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Leafy‑green allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific greens included in the blend.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Certain leafy greens are high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Thermal processing
items.content: The product is already cooked; additional heating may lead to further nutrient loss.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Greens, NS as to form, cooked can be added to soups, stews, smoothies, salads and omelets. It also works well as a base for purees or as a side dish for meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in its original packaging. Once opened, keep it for up to 5 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes colour.

content.title: About
content.content: Kale is a leafy cruciferous vegetable native to the Mediterranean and East Asia. It has a mildly bitter, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Raw kale is commonly used in salads, smoothies, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale belongs to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts.
There are several varieties, including curly kale and Lacinato (dinosaur) kale.
Kale was a staple food in Scandinavia during the Middle Ages and served as a winter reserve.
It contains more vitamin K per serving than any other leafy green.
Kale can grow in cold climates, even when temperatures drop below freezing.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Kale provides over 800% of the daily value for vitamin K, which is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: It is packed with carotenoids, vitamin C, and flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: The fiber in kale supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains calcium and iron
items.content: Kale offers a plant-based source of calcium and iron, important for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Its potassium content and low sodium level help regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Digestive difficulty
items.content: Raw kale leaves can be tough to digest; chopping finely or massaging the leaves can help.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K intake may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Kale contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw kale can be added to salads, smoothies, wraps, or made into "kale chips". Before use, wash the leaves thoroughly and slice them thinly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kale in the refrigerator in a bag or container with a small amount of moisture. It stays fresh for 5–7 days. Discard any leaves that become yellow or limp.

content.title: About
content.content: Orange chicken is an Asian‑inspired dish consisting of bite‑size pieces of chicken breast coated in a light batter, fried, and tossed in a sweet‑tart sauce made from orange juice, sugar, soy sauce, ginger, garlic and spices. It is a staple of many fusion restaurants and is often served with rice or noodles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was popularized in the United States in the 1980s as a Western adaptation of the Chinese "cheng ji" (orange chicken).
The combination of sweet orange sauce and a hint of heat from ginger makes it a favorite among children.
Natural orange zest or extract is often added to give the sauce a vivid color and fresh aroma.
Traditionally, the chicken is marinated in soy sauce and cornstarch before being fried to achieve a crisp coating.
It is commonly served as a one‑dish meal together with a vegetable side such as broccoli or carrots.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: The orange juice in the sauce provides a good amount of vitamin C, which supports immune function and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast supplies high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium from the orange component helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with a modest amount of oil, the dish contains little saturated fat.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Ginger and garlic in the sauce stimulate gastric juices, aiding digestion.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken, experiencing skin reactions or digestive upset.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The sweet sauce can raise the glycemic index of the meal, so people with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Soy sauce adds a notable amount of salt; those with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium soy sauce.

items.title: Frying oil
items.content: Deep‑frying in large amounts of oil can make the dish calorie‑dense and may introduce trans fats if non‑refined oils are used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve orange chicken hot, typically over steamed rice, noodles, or a vegetable side. The sauce can be poured over the chicken or used as a dip. For a lighter version, bake the chicken in the oven and toss with the sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a skillet or oven to retain the crisp coating. If the sauce thickens, thin it with a splash of water or orange juice.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans are a variety of common bean popular in Mexican and South American cuisines. In canned form they are pre‑cooked, and the reduced sodium (2143 mg/100 g) makes them suitable for low‑salt diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “pinto” comes from the Spanish word for “spotted,” referring to the bean’s mottled brown‑red skin.
Pinto beans are a key ingredient in traditional dishes such as fajitas and chili con carne.
Canned pinto beans can be stored for 3‑5 years without loss of flavor or nutritional value.
Reduced sodium is achieved by using a lower‑salt brine and adding potassium‑based salts.
Pinto beans are rich in plant protein and fiber, providing a sustained energy source.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: One cup of canned pinto beans provides about 15 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron supports oxygen transport, while folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell growth.

items.title: Reduced sodium content
items.content: Lower sodium is beneficial for individuals monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as polyphenols help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; rinsing canned beans before use mitigates this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal gas in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction reduces the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add pinto beans to salads, soups, chili, tacos, or use them as a filling for burritos. Before use, drain the liquid and rinse the beans under cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 4‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry Drink Syrup (5033) is a concentrated sweet syrup made from strawberries, intended for preparing non‑alcoholic drinks, cocktails and desserts. It has a bright red colour, the aroma of ripe strawberries and a rich fruity taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The syrup is produced from natural strawberry puree, sugar and citric acid.
Natural beet colour is often used to stabilise the vivid red hue.
One litre of syrup is enough to make about 10 litres of finished beverage.
The syrup can be used as a base for mocktails, fruit punches and ice‑cream.
In some countries it is added to yogurts and cottage‑cheese desserts to enhance flavour.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Strawberries are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins in strawberries help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A small amount of dietary fibre in the syrup may aid normal digestion.

items.title: Enhances flavour without artificial additives
items.content: Natural fruit aroma allows reduction of artificial flavourings.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The sugar in the syrup provides rapid energy, useful for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Strawberry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries or their components.

items.title: Not suitable for diabetics without adjustment
items.content: The syrup should be used cautiously by people with carbohydrate metabolism disorders.

items.title: Presence of preservatives
items.content: Certain versions may contain preservatives that are unsuitable for people with sensitivities.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dilute the syrup with water at a ratio of 1:10 (or to taste) to obtain a ready‑to‑drink beverage. Add to cocktails, punches, smoothies, yogurts, desserts, or use as a topping for ice‑cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the syrup in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and use within 3‑4 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Sugar NFS is a crystalline food-grade sugar derived from sugarcane or beet. It has a neutral sweet taste, high solubility in water, and is used in cooking, baking, and beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sugar is one of the oldest sweeteners, used for more than 5,000 years.
The term NFS (Non‑Food Sugar) indicates that the product meets strict food safety standards.
Its crystalline structure makes it easy to measure portions by weight.
Sugar caramelizes easily, creating aromatic brown tones.
When kept dry, sugar can be stored for a long time without quality loss.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Glucose in sugar is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Sugar amplifies taste perception, making dishes more enjoyable.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: In solutions, sugar helps retain water in the body, useful during intense exercise.

items.title: Blood sugar spikes
items.content: Excessive intake can cause hyperglycemia and contribute to diabetes development.

items.title: Dental caries
items.content: Sugar feeds oral bacteria that erode tooth enamel.

items.title: Weight gain
items.content: Sugar provides many calories without nutrients, which can lead to weight gain.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sugar NFS is suitable for sweetening drinks, baked goods, sauces, marinades, and desserts. It can be dissolved in hot or cold water, sprinkled on fruit, or used as a topping for pastries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sugar in an airtight container in a dry, cool place away from moisture and direct sunlight. If moisture gets in, crystals may clump together.
